title: Cottage cheese: protein, fat and calories

seo.title: Cottage cheese nutrition: protein, fat and calories
seo.meta_description: A current 2% cottage cheese has 19 g protein and 130 calories per 150 g. See how 2% and whole-milk versions change fat while protein stays high.
seo.search_intent: Understand cottage cheese protein, fat, calories and sodium

excerpt: Cottage cheese can deliver close to 20 g protein in one small cup. Good Culture 2% provides 19 g protein, 130 calories and 3 g fat per 150 g; its 4% whole-milk single serve also provides 19 g protein but 140 calories and 6 g fat. Sodium is often the number worth checking alongside protein.
content_html:
Cottage cheese is unusual among cheeses because it stays very moist. That lets it provide a lot of protein without the calorie density of a hard aged cheese.

A 2% single-serving example

Good Culture Simply 2% lists per 150 g:

  • 130 calories
  • 19 g protein
  • 3 g fat
  • 5 g total sugars, 0 g added
  • 520 mg sodium
  • 140 mg calcium

That works out to about 12.7 g protein per 100 g.

What changes in whole-milk cottage cheese?

The same brand's 4% single serve still contains 19 g protein per 150 g, but fat rises to 6 g and calories to 140. Protein remains essentially unchanged while richness increases.

Why protein is high

Cottage cheese is made by forming milk curds and retaining them in a moist creamy dressing rather than pressing and aging them into a dry block. The curds are rich in casein protein.

Watch sodium

The 150 g examples contain about 520 mg sodium. Cottage cheese can therefore be much saltier than plain yogurt or skyr even when calories and protein look similar.

It is not automatically a “low-calorie cheese”

Cottage cheese retains a lot of water, which usually keeps its energy density below aged cheeses. But the creamy dressing can be made with different amounts of fat, so regular and low-fat versions are not nutritionally interchangeable.

The useful label reading is combined: protein, fat, sodium and serving size. A 150 g serving can provide more than 20 g of protein, but the cited products can also contribute around 1.2 g of salt-equivalent sodium. Both numbers belong in the same decision.

How to compare cottage cheese beyond the protein number

The label matters unusually much with cottage cheese because fat level and formulation vary across products. Two tubs may provide similar protein yet differ in calories, total fat, saturated fat, sodium, and serving size. Comparing per 100 grams is useful for nutrient density; comparing the portion you actually eat is useful for understanding a meal. Higher-fat versions are often creamier, while low-fat versions can have a different texture. Neither category is automatically the right choice for every person or every recipe.

Sodium deserves particular attention because cottage cheese is fresh but not necessarily low in salt. If it is a frequent food, a lower-sodium option can make a meaningful difference for someone whose overall diet is already salt-heavy. Flavored products may also add sugars, fruit preparations, or other ingredients that change calories and carbohydrate. Cottage cheese can work in toast, salads, bowls, baked potatoes, or with fruit, but the satiety and nutritional value of the meal depend on everything served with it. Protein is a genuine strength; it does not need to become the only number used to choose a tub.

How much protein is in cottage cheese? The 2% and 4% single-serve examples here both provide 19 g per 150 g.

How many calories does cottage cheese have? 130 calories per 150 g for the 2% example and 140 for the 4% whole-milk version.

Does higher fat mean more protein? Not in these products. Both provide 19 g protein; the main change is fat.

Is cottage cheese high in sodium? It can be. These single-serve examples contain about 520 mg per 150 g.

Cottage cheese can also vary in texture because curd size, cream dressing, stabilizers, and moisture differ by brand. A higher-protein label does not necessarily mean the product will be thicker or more filling for every person, and low-fat versions are not automatically lower in sodium. Decide what matters for the meal: a snack may benefit from fruit and nuts for fiber and texture, while a savory bowl can be combined with vegetables, herbs, or whole-grain toast. Looking at the whole meal prevents one nutrient number from carrying more meaning than it should.

How cottage cheese is eaten changes its role. Paired with fruit and nuts it can become a substantial snack; with tomatoes, herbs, and whole-grain toast it works as a savory meal component. Those additions contribute fiber, fats, and carbohydrates that cottage cheese itself provides in smaller amounts, so the finished bowl can be more balanced than the dairy product on its own.

How to choose a tub

Compare protein, milkfat percentage and sodium. A lower-fat cottage cheese can save some calories while keeping protein high, but the exact numbers depend on the recipe.
